← Interior door bid calculator

How much to charge to replace interior doors

Carpenters get shopped on a published $150 a door installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the opening or the leaf. A hollow-core slab hung on an existing jamb is a different job from a solid-core prehung in a new opening with paint-grade casing, new privacy hardware, and a haul-away.

Open the free interior door bid calculator

Price the opening and the leaf, not the $150 dump

An interior door replacement is an opening, then a leaf, then how ready that jamb is. Hollow slab is a cheap leaf. Hollow prehung is a builder unit. Solid-core is weight. French-or-barn is a pair of leaves or a track. Hang-only hangs a slab on the existing jamb. Prehung-swap pulls the old unit. New-opening is a header. Pocket-conversion is a wall pocket.

Hollow slab versus solid-core on the same opening

Homeowners usually start from the hollow-slab special, then ask whether solid-core, 8-foot, or a French pair is “a little more.” On the same opening and the same scope it is not a little more. Solid-core buys a heavier leaf and a closer fit. French-or-barn is a pair and hardware. The calculator prices all four leaves on the opening you already counted so you can quote the upgrade instead of matching the hollow-slab number on a French-pair job.

Hang-only is not a pocket conversion

The cheap special is almost always an 80-inch hollow slab, no paint, no haul, no frame work. A French-pair pocket conversion is a different crew hour. Matching an installed number on a pocket-frame job is how a sold door becomes a loss when the header and the extra trip eat the margin.

This is not an entry door, a slider, or a garage door

An entry door is weather, sidelights, a transom, and jamb-rot. A patio slider is panels and impact glass. A garage door is springs and a header. Plantation shutters are louvered panels. Crown molding is a run of trim. Interior painting is a coat. This prices an interior door replacement: the leaf, the opening, the casing, and extras.

Customer-supplied leaves are not a free hang

Owners also shop a second special: “I already bought it — just hang it for $150.” Zeroing the millwork invoice drops the bid. The trip and the set stay. A slab that binds is a second trip. See should I hang a customer-supplied door for the three-way comparison on the same opening.

Saturday is not the weekday bid

A third special is the calendar: “Can you come Saturday? Same $150?” After-hours is time-and-a-half plus a second dispatch. Weekday while they stay home is the same wage on a slower hang. See should I hang doors on Saturday for weekday they-leave versus they-stay versus after-hours on the same opening.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the interior door bid calculator. It is not a building-code determination, a fire-rating specification, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to replace interior doors?

Charge from door count, leaf, size, scope, extras, and when you can work — not a published $150-a-door installed special. A hollow-core slab hung on an existing jamb is a different job from a solid-core prehung in a new opening with paint-grade casing, new privacy hardware, and a haul-away.

Is hang-only the same bid as a pocket-conversion door?

No. Hang-only hangs a slab on the existing jamb. Prehung-swap pulls the old unit and sets a new prehung. New-opening is a header and studs. Pocket-conversion is a wall pocket. Matching an installed special on a pocket-conversion job is how a sold door becomes a loss when the header and the extra trip eat the margin.

How do solid-core, 8-foot, and a French pair change an interior-door price?

Hollow slab is a cheap leaf. Hollow prehung is a builder unit. Solid-core is weight. French-or-barn is a pair of leaves or a track. Price all four on the same opening to see the upgrade — matching the hollow-slab special on a French-pair job is the losing bid. Paint, haul-away, and a new lockset do not live in a published installed dump.

Is Saturday the same bid as a weekday they-leave hang?

No. After-hours is time-and-a-half plus a second dispatch. A $349 Saturday special on a hollow-slab hang covers a weekday they-leave slot and loses money after hours. See should I hang doors on Saturday.

Is this the same as an entry door, a patio slider, or a garage door?

No. An entry door is weather, sidelights, a transom, and jamb-rot. A patio slider is panels and impact glass. A garage door is springs and a header. This prices an interior door replacement: the leaf, the opening, the casing, and extras.

    Common questions

    Why can a flyer advertise “$150 a door installed”?

    Because that number describes one specific job, and it is the first preset here: a hollow-core slab hung on an existing jamb, 80-inch single opening, no paint, no haul-away, no hardware upgrade. Hang-only bills 0.75 hours of hang labor and a $48 door invoice — genuinely close to $150 installed. A prehung swap, a new framed opening, or a pocket conversion is a different job with its own framing and casing hours, and the flyer’s number was never written to cover them.

    Why does a pocket conversion cost so much more than a prehung swap?

    Because it is framing a wall cavity, not swapping a unit. A prehung swap bills 1.4 hours to hang, 0.3 to frame, and a $0 frame kit. A pocket conversion bills 1.8 hours to hang, 3.4 hours to frame, and a $240 frame kit on top of $68 of casing — more than ten times the framing labor of a swap, before the door leaf itself is counted.

    What does the door type change beyond the invoice?

    Both labor and material move together. A hollow-core slab adds zero extra hours and a $48 invoice. A hollow-core prehung unit adds 0.15 hours and $175. A solid-core prehung adds 0.5 hours — it is heavier to hang and shim — and $340. A French pair or barn door adds 1.15 hours and $720, since it is effectively two leaves or a track system instead of one swinging slab.

    Why does an 8-foot or double door cost more than the standard 80-inch single?

    Height and leaf count each carry their own hours and hardware cost, on top of whatever the door type already bills. A 96-inch single adds 0.55 hours and a $95 extra-leaf charge for the taller jamb and casing run. A double opening adds 0.9 hours and $175, since it is two leaves and two sets of hardware in one frame.

    What do paint, haul-away, and hardware upgrades add per door?

    Each is billed per door, not as a flat job fee, so they scale with door count the way a whole- house order actually does. Skipping them on a single-door swap barely moves the price; skipping them on an eight-door whole-house job is the difference between a painter’s punch list and a finished room.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

Should I hang a customer-supplied door?

Owners call with a slab in the hallway: “I already bought the door. Can you just hang it for $150?” That sounds like free margin because the millwork invoice left the bid. It did not leave the trip, the hang hours, or the chance that the leaf is a 30-inch in a 32-inch jamb.

Open the free interior door bid calculator

Zeroing the leaf is not a free hang

A carpenter-supplied hollow slab still carries the millwork invoice. An owner-supplied leaf that actually hangs zeros that line and keeps the same set hours. On a typical 80-inch hang-only — $42 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, six miles — the carpenter-supplied bid is in the mid-$300s. Zeroing a $48 slab drops it, but the owner-supplied walk-away stays above $150. Taking the Facebook special to “just hang what they bought” still loses money.

Hang hoursSameSameSame, plus a callback
At $150 hang-onlyLosesStill losesLoses more

Wrong size is a second trip

Store shelves default to 80-inch by 24/28/30/32. Plenty of jambs are 96-inch, a pair, or a hair tight. Hanging the wrong slab means a plane pass or a drive back to exchange it. Price that callback on the same opening before you agree. The calculator adds a starting second trip and a plane/shim kit on top of the rates you already typed.

How to use the comparison

Open the interior door bid calculator, enter the opening you are standing in, and put their hang-only number in “price you’re considering.” The who-supplies table scores that number against you-supply, owner-supplies-it-hangs, and owner-supplies-wrong-size. Nothing is uploaded.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to replace interior doors. It is not a building-code determination, a fire-rating specification, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each supply path.

Common questions

Should I hang an interior door the customer bought at a store?

Only after you price the hang without the millwork invoice. Pulling their slab is still a trip, a set, and crew hours. A $150 hang-only special often sits under that walk-away number even when the leaf is free to you.

Does a customer-supplied door make the $150 installed special profitable?

Usually not. Zeroing a $48 hollow-slab invoice drops the bid, but loaded labor, travel, and overhead stay. On a typical 80-inch hang-only the owner-supplied walk-away is still above $150. A slab that binds or is the wrong height adds a second trip and a plane pass.

What if the store-bought slab is the wrong height or binds in the jamb?

That is a second dispatch plus a plane and shim, or a drive back to exchange it. Price that callback on the same opening before you agree to hang whatever they rolled into the driveway. The calculator adds a starting callback trip and a plane kit on top of your current rates.

Should I hang doors on Saturday?

Open the free interior door bid calculator

vs-a-flat-per-door-price.html.text:
← Interior Door Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-door price

"$150 a door installed" is not a price for an opening — it is a price for whatever job the special was built on, quietly applied to a pocket conversion with a French pair.

What a flat per-door price is

A flat per-door number is the fastest way to quote a door job over the phone: ask how many doors, multiply by the special, skip the walkthrough. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between carpenters, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — usually a hollow-core slab hung on an existing jamb — and then reused for every door afterward, whether or not the next opening needs framing, a heavier leaf, a taller or double size, or paint and a haul-away.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the door count, the scope (hang-only, prehung-swap, new-opening, or pocket-conversion), the leaf (hollow slab, hollow prehung, solid-core, or French-or-barn), the size (80-inch, 96-inch, or double), and whether paint, haul-away, and new hardware are included, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It prices the hang, frame, and casing hours by scope, adds the leaf and extras invoices, and returns the walk-away price and the price per door — for this opening, not a generic count.

What a flat per-door price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a hollow-slab hang and a French-pair pocket conversion — even though one is a slab on an existing jamb and the other is a framed wall opening. Prices frame, casing, and hang hours separately by scope, so a new opening or a pocket costs more than a hang-only swap.
Has no line for the leaf itself, regardless of whether it is a $48 hollow slab or a $720 French-or-barn unit. Prices the leaf invoice by door type, plus an extra-leaf charge for a 96-inch or double opening.
Has no line for paint, haul-away, or a new lockset, regardless of how many of them the job needs. Prices paint, haul-away, and hardware hours and invoices per door, only when each is included.
Estimates travel by eye, with no separate check against trip time or mileage. Prices trip hours plus mileage as loaded labor, on top of the per-door work.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat per-door price would have quoted, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two doors, the same flat quote

Using this calculator's own shipped starting examples:

A single hollow-core slab hung on an existing 80-inch jamb prices at $339.14 with a 20% target margin, on a job that costs $271.31 to run — already above a flat $150 quote before any scope changes at all.

Frame that same single opening as a pocket conversion instead, for a French-or-barn pair at 96 inches, with paint, haul-away, and new hardware included, and the job costs $2,258.93 to run before a dollar of profit — almost entirely the frame kit, the leaf, and the extra labor hours a pocket wall needs. The same flat $150-a-door quote that already undercut the easy hang is $2,108.93 below this job's own break-even cost, before counting the $2,673.66 it falls short of this calculator's own bid price at a 20% target margin. Same door count, same flat rate, one opening that barely clears the number and one that loses well over two thousand dollars the moment the header goes in.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-door price get an interior-door quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is the scope and the leaf, not the count of doors. A hollow-core slab hung on an existing jamb and a French pair framed into a new pocket wall are both "one door," but one is 0.75 hours of hanging and a $48 leaf while the other is a framed pocket, a heavier leaf, paint, a haul-away, and new hardware. A flat per-door price charges both the same.

What does a flat per-door price usually leave out entirely?

The scope. A per-door number has no line for framing a new opening or a wall pocket, no line for the jump from a hollow slab to a solid-core or French-or-barn leaf, no line for an 8-foot or double opening needing more casing, and no line for paint, haul-away, or a new lockset -- each its own hours and its own invoice.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own worked examples: a hang-only hollow-slab door at 80 inches costs $271.31 to run and prices at $339.14 with a 20% target margin -- already above a flat $150 quote before scope changes at all. Framing the same single opening as a pocket conversion for a French-or-barn pair at 96 inches, with paint, haul-away, and new hardware, costs $2,258.93 to run and prices at $2,823.66. The same $150 quote that already falls short on the easy hang is $2,108.93 below the pocket-conversion job's own break-even cost -- before a dollar of profit.

Is a flat per-door price ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- hang-only swaps on existing jambs, the same leaf and size every time -- a per-door number can land close, because that is probably the job it was built on. The risk is applying it to a job with a new opening, a pocket wall, a heavier leaf, or extras mixed in without pricing the scope separately, because the flat number does not know what the opening needs and neither does the estimator until the wall is already open.

Does this calculator know what door leaf costs or labor rates are in my market?

No. It has no data on your local millwork supplier's prices or your local labor market. It takes the door count, scope, leaf, size, and extras you choose, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this opening -- the arithmetic a flat per-door price skips, not a market survey.

Open the Interior Door Bid Calculator to price your own opening, or read how much to charge to replace interior doors.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own supplier invoices, payroll, insurance, and overhead, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. ← Interior Door Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business. This page is a free, private worksheet for one interior door replacement before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the scope (hang-only on an existing jamb, a prehung swap, framing a new opening, or a pocket conversion), the door type (hollow slab, hollow prehung, solid-core, or French-or-barn), paint, haul-away, and a new lockset, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a copyable customer-facing bid summary, and a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
